The capacity in the model was set to match the serpentine component, and the flow rates and temperature differences across each fluid stream were set to match the experimental targets. The experimental serpentine results are compared to the microchannel model results in Figure 20 while only discharging the device (charge circuit was turned off). The results are similar, with the microchannel device performing slightly better, particularly at high power rates. For example, at 1.51 C (5.3 kW) the microchannel component can extract nearly 3 kWh of capacity from the component, whereas the serpentine device can only use about 2 kWh before it reaches the cutoff. Figure 20: Discharge experiments: Comparison between the discharge circuit fluid outlet temperatures (a) experimentally measured in the serpentine design and (b) modeled with the validated microchannel finite difference simulation. The discharge power and capacity before the outlet temperature reaches the cutoff (16°C) in the (c) serpentine experiments and from the (d) microchannel model are also shown. The microchannel design has a larger impact when the device is discharged in hybrid mode, as shown in Figure 21. Again, the capacity, flow rates and temperature differences from the serpentine experiments were used in the microchannel model to compare their performance. In this case, the microchannel design performs sustainably better because of the good thermal contact between fluid channels. The charge fluid inlet temperature (blue line in Figure 21 a and b) is much higher than the serpentine design, meaning that the efficiency of the charging system will improve with the new component. Additionally, the discharge circuit outlet temperature remains below the cutoff temperature for longer, which will result in a high useable system capacity. 21 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications. Task 5: Building modeling and scenario simulations Task Summary: With updated thermal storage module and HVAC system models, NREL will run building simulations for different scenarios. These modeling results will be used to update target market locations and economic estimates. We investigated the performance of the hybrid TES RTU for a retail strip mall building. This included two climates: Los Angeles, CA (climate zone 3B), a hot climate with relatively large diurnal temperature swings, and Baltimore, MD (climate zone 4A), a warm/humid climate with smaller diurnal temperature swings.
